Menopause Was a Hushed Conversation—Until Gen X Changed Everything

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1550 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sharon Cancio, 28, didn’t grow up knowing much about menopause.
  • It has been revealed that cancio didn’t start connecting the dots until she came off birth control at 25 and noticed how dramatically her own mood changed around her cycle.
  • These discussions are a far cry from what conversations around menopause used to look like: nonexistent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sharon Cancio, 28, didn’t grow up knowing much about menopause. She didn’t learn anything about it in school, nor from the women in her family. But when she was a teenager, she started noticing her mother’s mood shifting. Around her mid-to-late 40s, “she became much snappier, more easily irritated, and sometimes just seemed angry in a way that felt completely different from the mom I remembered growing up,” she recalls. “I genuinely thought life had simply worn her down.”.

It has been revealed that cancio didn’t start connecting the dots until she came off birth control at 25 and noticed how dramatically her own mood changed around her cycle. Once she realized her mother had entered perimenopause, she went down an internet rabbit hole to learn about it. Women were discussing—in detail—what was happening to their bodies on TikTok and Reddit. Some women were going through menopause early, others were seeking answers for their symptoms.

These discussions are a far cry from what conversations around menopause used to look like: nonexistent. In the past, there wasn’t much education—or even real discussion—on what happens to the female body after 40, forcing women to hustle through hot flashes and mood swings behind closed doors.

But within the last few years, there’s been a shift: Gen X women are the first to go through this hormonal transition in the age of social media—and they’re not afraid to talk about their experiences, states Gillan Goddard, MD, an endocrinologist and an adjunct assistant professor of medicine at the NYU Langone Hospital. They’re educating an entire generation of younger women in the process. Posts about brain fog, inconsistent sleep patterns, and unfamiliar-feeling bodies have become the first real health literacy that this generation’s daughters, Gen Zers, have gotten about their own hormonal futures. These small conversations have big implications when it comes to learning more about their future health.

Industry observers note that the lack of menopause education starts in classrooms: Almost all U.S. states require teenagers to learn about puberty, reproductive health, and sexual disease prevention through sex education classes. But the content and depth of those classes may not favor women’s health: A 2024 study in the Journal of School Health looked at the state of menstrual health education in U.S. K-12 public schools. Researchers analyzed the education standards from each state’s Department of Education site, searching terms like “menstruation,” “menopause,” “period,” “reproduction,” and “puberty.” It found that menstrual health education—especially menopause—is profoundly rare.

There’s also a lack of menopause education in medical schools. Only 31.3 percent of U.S. ob-gyn residency programs include a menopause curriculum, according to a 2023 study in Menopause. The result resembles a serious disconnect: The transition affects nearly half of the population, but the majority of the doctors tasked with treating menopause have received almost no training on how to do it.

Recent findings suggest that menopause just isn’t prioritized during residency training. Instead, the “focus during training was placed on surgical skills and labor and delivery responsibilities, both considered more urgent and time-consuming,” notes Alyssa Dweck, MD, chief medical officer of Bonafide Health and a Menopause Society Certified Practitioner located in New York City. Ob-gyns can earn certifications in (peri)menopause, from organizations including the Menopause Society and Integrative Women’s Health Institute—but they’re not required. Clinicians should have more comprehensive training in medical school and beyond, says Dr. Dweck. But there should also be more funding and resources for women’s health research for treatment options.

When doctors aren’t familiar with menopause, “mood changes, cognitive changes, and body aches are often misunderstood or ignored,” says Dr. Goddard. This can lead to misdiagnoses, and to women not receiving proper treatment for symptoms caused by menopause. This is pretty common: A 2025 survey conducted by health care tech giant Biote of over 1,000 women ages 30 to 60 in the U.S. found that 39 percent of women have been misdiagnosed and prescribed medication by a provider for conditions like depression.

Recent findings suggest that tikTok and Instagram have filled the menopause education void in the U.S. Conversations about life in menopause have spread awareness about what the condition is actually like, crushing stigmas. This visibility is not only helping younger viewers learn what they can expect later in life—it’s also helping mothers start more health-forward conversations with their daughters.

Milan Parker, 25, has always had open conversations about health with her mom. “She’s always been really honest with me about what she’s going through, even the more personal parts that people sometimes consider taboo,” she claims. But social media increased this dynamic tenfold: Parker’s mother underwent a hysterectomy due to fibroids at 48, which made her enter early menopause. Following the surgery, her mother joined a menopause support group on Facebook. “Seeing that there were women all across the country going through similar things made her more open to talking to me about it,” Parker says.

For instance, Parker’s mom finally explained how debilitating her hot flashes really were. (She’d stopped going on trips with her because she was embarrassed about looking sweaty.) “There were times when I thought maybe my mom just didn’t want to go out with me,” she says. “I’m really grateful that she made it something we could actually talk about instead of something that had to stay a secret.”.

Sources indicate that for daughters, it can be hard to watch their mothers struggle in menopause and not know how to help, but the experience can also help them grow closer. “The emotional experience can be a mix of empathy, grief, anxiety, and closeness,” says Ashley Peña, LCSW, a clinical social worker and the vice president of outpatient operations at A Mission for Michael.

Industry observers note that even though Cancio’s mom didn’t tell her when she was going through menopause, the experience helped her gain compassion for her mother and better understand her own body. “As a teenager, I honestly thought she was just becoming grumpy or ‘getting old,’ which I feel terrible admitting now,” she claims. “As an adult woman, I have so much more empathy.”.

Having a raw look at what menopause is actually like—whether through a screen or a conversation with their mother—shapes how younger women view aging and how to prepare themselves for what’s ahead. Hearing that they may one day inevitably experience sleepless nights, sudden anger, brain fog, and the loss of identity can be scary, to say the least. But “open conversation about menopause helps women hear the full scope of menopause experiences and how women dealt effectively with their symptoms,” Dr. Goddard indicates. It can make the condition sound less scary to younger women.

In a recent development, in fact, growing conversations around menopause can actually inspire younger women to learn about it earlier. “I am seeing patients of all ages, Gen Z included, who have become more inquisitive and engaged in their health overall,” Dr. Dweck says. Some of her young patients have told her they’ve already started talking to their older relatives about menopause and hormone health. They’re also more open about discussing fertility and egg freezing.

Even though menopause is now common dinner table conversation, the root of the (non-communication) concern still needs to be fixed. “The only way we normalize talking about women’s health is by talking about it,” Cancio notes. “Ask questions, stay curious, and don’t be afraid to learn from women who have already been through it.”.

Mothers going through (peri)menopause can have a series of casual conversations about it with their kids. (The earlier, the better.) They can keep the conversation casual and tailored to the child’s developmental age. For instance, moms with children under the age of 13 can briefly mention that they’re “going through a body change.” Then, as the kids get older, they can talk more openly about what they’re experiencing, notes Dr. Dweck. Encouraging their children to ask questions about menopause can also build empathy and normalize conversations surrounding health.

In a recent development, on the flip side, Parker wants Gen Z women to pay attention to what their mothers are going through, and not wait until the right moment to spark a conversation. “Having those conversations with my mom has made that feel a lot less scary and a lot more human,” she indicates. “Every stage of life comes sooner than you think, so it’s worth paying attention to your health long before you feel like you have to.”.

Cancio didn’t feel like she could have those conversations with her mom, which is part of what inspired her to start making content around women’s health topics for younger women. “I started thinking about the girl who was sitting at home Googling something because she was too embarrassed to ask her mom, or the girl who thought something was wrong with her because nobody had ever explained that what she was experiencing was normal,” she states.

It has been revealed that even though the way that Gen Z is learning about menopause isn’t perfect—whether through a viral post or their mother—it’s still a step in the right direction. By doing her part, Cancio hopes to have a completely different relationship with her future daughter “where no topic about her body is off limits and she never feels like she has to search for answers alone.”.

#52335. Why We Learn More From What Goes Right

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1054 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Why We Learn More From What Goes Right

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Conventional wisdom states that we learn more from failure than success, and our culture tends to support this, often romanticizing failure as a noble precursor to accomplishment.
  • We know that globally, around 70 to 80 percent of business start-ups fail within 10 years, varying by industry and region.
  • It has been revealed that in other words, in the case of a start-up business, experience of success is four times more valuable than experience of failure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

Conventional wisdom states that we learn more from failure than success, and our culture tends to support this, often romanticizing failure as a noble precursor to accomplishment. Business literature encourages us to “fail forward” or “fail better”—phrases that have become as ubiquitous as they are clichéd.

We know that globally, around 70 to 80 percent of business start-ups fail within 10 years, varying by industry and region. But wherever you go, the chances of failure of a start-up are overwhelmingly greater than the probability of success. Take the example of 80 in 100 new businesses ultimately failing—that means there are 20 recipes for success and 80 for failure. If you succeed, you have discovered one of the 20 routes to success, whereas if you fail, you have experienced one of the 80 routes to failure.

It has been revealed that in other words, in the case of a start-up business, experience of success is four times more valuable than experience of failure. Success will always be more instructive than failure when the probability of success is less than that of failure, which is virtually always the case in endeavors of impact and scale. They are never easy.

We are told that failure breeds resilience. Winston Churchill famously said, “Success is going from failure to failure without losing enthusiasm.” While that made sense in the bleak early days of World War II, when successes on the battlefield were rare, overall failure is overrated as a staging post on the path to success.

To be clear: I am not saying we can’t learn from failure, or that bouncing back from it isn’t hugely commendable and character-building. Importantly, the courage to fail emboldens people to try, and this is the bedrock of entrepreneurship and ultimately economic growth. But at an individual level, success is a better teacher.

At Discovery, we have learned from both success and failure, but our most profound lessons have come from learning what went right.

In 2008, we exited the U.S. health insurance market after eight years of trying to gain traction. Despite our efforts, we couldn’t attract enough members to create the scale to compete with incumbent giants. It was a very painful and instructive failure. And yes, we learned lessons that helped propel us onto the global stage. Today, instead of competing head-on, we partner with global insurers.

Recent findings suggest that but what has been the biggest cause of our progress? Is it learning from our failure in the U.S.? Or is it the insights drawn from our success in incentivizing healthier behavior and turning that into a scalable global model known as Vitality?

In a recent development, both have been important. But in my view, the lessons from success have been more transformative.

According to recent reports, the reasons why we learn more from success than failure lie in our psychology. Emotionally, failure is difficult to absorb. It feels bad. And when something feels bad, we tune out and don’t absorb the lessons as deeply.

Behavioral science reveals that people tend to avoid personal bad news. For example, various studies show that up to 54 percent of individuals who undergo an HIV diagnostic test will not collect their results.

Cognitively, failure yields less useful information than success. Whereas success reveals patterns and principles that can be replicated, failure tends to be less instructional—it tells us what not to do but rarely illuminates what we should do.

Research by American motivational psychologists Lauren Eskreis-Winkler and Ayelet Fishbach, who aim to better understand the nature of success by studying failure, found that failure undermines learning. In their 2019 paper, “Not Learning from Failure—The Greatest Failure of All,” they reported on five studies with over 1,600 participants, who were asked a series of binary choice questions. For example: How much money do U.S. companies lose annually due to poor customer service? They were given only two possible answers to choose from: $60 billion or $90 billion. They were then given the correct answers to all questions and re-tested. Given that there were only two possible answers in each case, participants ought to have been able to remember the right one. But those who got the answer correct the first time did better on re-testing than those who got it wrong the first time. Why?

Industry observers note that “Our society celebrates failure as a teachable moment,” they wrote. “Yet in five studies, failure did the opposite: it undermined learning. Why does failure undermine learning? Failure is ego-threatening, which causes people to tune out.”.

In the field of medicine, a fascinating study from Harvard Business School—“Learning From My Success and From Others’ Failure”—tracked 71 cardiothoracic surgeons over 10 years and 6,500 operations. The research, by KC Diwas and colleagues, found that surgeons learned more from their own successes than from their own failures—and more from others’ mistakes than others’ successes. Why? Because others’ failures don’t trigger the same ego threat, so we tune in more readily.

Ironically, while failure demands resilience, it doesn’t always build it. Success does. It reminds us that winning and progress are possible.

Recent findings suggest that of course, there are times when failure is immensely instructive. Plane crashes happen so rarely that when they do, they present rich opportunities for learning. If you are flying a space shuttle, you are only as strong as your weakest link, and studying these allows you to avoid the same catastrophic outcome twice.

But in complex networked systems, where processes are not linear, and where the chances of failure are greater than the chances of success, it is success that teaches best.

In a recent development, gutiérrez, E., M. C. Iglesias, F. J. Quezada-Juarez, E. Rodríguez-Estrada, G. Reyes-Terán, and N. P. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Latest research suggests that caffeinated energy drinks and stimulant supplements are associated with significantly higher risks of serious heart problems, including cardiac arrest and heart attack in young adults.
  • The findings, to be presented at the American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions 2026 November 6–9 in Chicago, are preliminary and can’t prove that energy drinks cause heart problems.
  • Still, the results highlight concerning cardiovascular effects of these popular products, particularly among adults under 35 who consume them regularly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest research suggests that caffeinated energy drinks and stimulant supplements are associated with significantly higher risks of serious heart problems, including cardiac arrest and heart attack in young adults.

The findings, to be presented at the American Heart Association (AHA) Scientific Sessions 2026 November 6–9 in Chicago, are preliminary and can’t prove that energy drinks cause heart problems.

Still, the results highlight concerning cardiovascular effects of these popular products, particularly among adults under 35 who consume them regularly.

“These products are marketed as everyday pick-me-ups and sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk,” study author Sai Samayamanthula, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Virginia School of Medicine in Charlottesville, VA, said in a news release.

“For many healthy people, if these products are consumed occasionally, the risk is probably small. However, individuals who consume energy drinks or other stimulant-containing supplements regularly can promptly exceed the recommended daily limit for caffeine, so it’s important for people to know that there may be a risk of cardiovascular harm with these products,” Samayamanthula continued.

Researchers from the University of Virginia School of Medicine analyzed 28,345 reports submitted to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) between 2017 and 2025.

Of these, 854 involved caffeinated energy drinks or stimulant supplements, while the remaining reports involved non-stimulant products.

In a recent development, compared with non-stimulant products, cardiac arrest was reported approximately 11 times more often with energy drinks and stimulant supplements. Heart attacks were reported 4.5 times more often, while ventricular arrhythmias and palpitations were reported about four times more frequently.

Nearly 45% of heart-related reports involved adults ages 18 to 34.

Recent findings suggest that “Our findings support the case for more systematic safety monitoring of caffeine- and stimulant-containing products. In addition, healthcare professionals should remember to ask their younger patients who have palpitations, chest pain or fainting spells if they recently or regularly consume these products,” Samayamanthula said.

In a recent development, gregory M. Marcus, MD, professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine, and chair of the 2026 AHA scientific statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease, wasn’t involved in the study, but remarked the research “raises concerns that products with very high amounts of caffeine may be harmful to the cardiovascular system.”.

“Although there are biological reasons why that connection could be possible, the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events, because other factors may have influenced the results found in this analysis,” Marcus noted in a news release.

“More research is needed to understand whether these stimulant products are truly responsible for the reported heart-related events.”.

Cheng-Han Chen, MD, board certified interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA, stated the findings, although concerning, are not surprising. Chen wasn’t involved in the study.

“We know that energy drinks can have significant effects on the cardiovascular system, primarily because of their stimulant properties,” he told Healthline.

In a recent development, “Caffeine can increase blood pressure and heart rate, while other ingredients, such as guarana and taurine, may further contribute to cardiovascular stimulation and increased stress hormone levels. What is particularly concerning is the potential for these products to trigger serious complications, including abnormal heart rhythms, especially in people with underlying cardiovascular conditions.”.

In a recent development, chen agreed that occasional energy drink consumption is unlikely to have long-term consequences for heart health in most healthy individuals. However, he noted that “frequent or excessive consumption can potentially increase the risk of hypertension and cardiac arrhythmias.”.

According to recent reports, an AHA scientific statement published in July 2026 notes that up to 400 milligrams of caffeine daily is generally considered safe for most healthy adults. That’s roughly equivalent to four or five 8-ounce cups of brewed coffee, depending on how it’s prepared.

However, some energy drinks contain up to three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce as brewed coffee.

Certain energy drinks may also contain stimulants, such as guarana, yerba mate, theobromine, synephrine, and yohimbine.

These ingredients may compound caffeine’s effects on the cardiovascular system.

Sources indicate that “Caffeine stimulates the cardiovascular system, primarily by increasing sympathetic nervous system activity. This can cause the heart to beat faster, raise blood pressure, and increase the workload on the heart,” Chen noted.

Industry observers note that “Energy drinks may contain additional stimulants, such as guarana and taurine, which can further increase blood pressure and stress hormone levels. With excessive consumption, these effects can become more pronounced and potentially interfere with the heart’s normal electrical activity, increasing the risk of abnormal heart rhythms. People with underlying cardiovascular conditions, particularly hypertension or a predisposition to arrhythmias, may be especially vulnerable to these effects.”.

It has been revealed that other research has echoed these concerns. A 2025 review suggests that high-volume energy drink consumption can prolong the heart’s QTc interval, increase blood pressure, and raise heart rate beyond the effects of caffeine alone.

“There is growing concern about the cardiovascular effects of energy drinks and stimulant-containing supplements, particularly among younger adults,” Chen stated.

“One challenge is that younger individuals may not recognize that these products can have significant effects on their heart and blood pressure, especially when consumed frequently or in combination with other caffeinated products.”.

Young adults accounted for a substantial portion of the FDA reports included in the study, highlighting potential cardiovascular concerns for this age group.

Sources indicate that people with existing heart conditions, a history of irregular heart rhythms, or heightened caffeine sensitivity may face additional risks. Those with undiagnosed genetic heart conditions may also be vulnerable.

A 2024 study identified cases of sudden cardiac arrest occurring shortly after energy drink consumption, particularly among people with underlying inherited heart conditions.

“As a cardiologist, I am particularly concerned about people who may have underlying cardiovascular conditions that have not yet been diagnosed,” Chen said.

Sources indicate that “Excessive stimulant intake can potentially trigger symptoms such as palpitations, chest discomfort, and lightheadedness. In susceptible individuals, it may also increase the risk of more serious complications, including abnormal heart rhythms.”.

Additionally, combining energy drinks with strenuous exercise or alcohol may introduce additional cardiovascular risks.

The findings suggest an association between energy drinks, stimulant supplements, and reported cardiovascular events, but they are preliminary and do not establish cause and effect.

The FDA database also relied on voluntary adverse-event reports, meaning some events may never be reported, while others may receive disproportionate attention.

Industry observers note that researchers also do not yet know how many people consumed these products without experiencing any problems. Without this variable, the reports cannot establish actual risk.

Other factors, including underlying health conditions, medications, and lifestyle habits, may also influence the results. More systematic research and controlled clinical trials are needed.

For most healthy adults, consuming up to 400 milligrams of caffeine per day is generally considered safe.

However, Chen noted that individual tolerance for caffeine may vary, and people with underlying cardiovascular conditions, particularly high blood pressure or abnormal heart rhythms, may need to limit or avoid caffeine altogether.

“Energy drinks can vary considerably in their caffeine content and serving sizes,” Chen stated.

In a recent development, “Depending on the product, a single can may contain anywhere from 80 to 300 milligrams of caffeine. This means that consuming even one or two energy drinks can put someone close to or above the recommended daily limit, particularly when combined with coffee, tea, or other caffeinated supplements.”.

Seek emergency medical attention if you experience chest pain, particularly if it’s accompanied by shortness of breath, fainting, or other symptoms of a possible heart attack.

If you live with a heart condition, ask your doctor about your daily caffeine intake to determine whether you need to cut back.

According to Chen, warning signs of excessive stimulant intake may include:.

“Depending on the severity of these symptoms, medical attention may be necessary,” he said.

It has been revealed that still, most people may not need to give up caffeine entirely. Monitoring your habits could help protect your heart health. This may include:.

“I encourage people to read product labels carefully and be aware of their total daily caffeine consumption,” Chen said. “I particularly recommend that people with underlying cardiovascular conditions avoid energy drinks.”.

Sources indicate that the KEI-01 will reintroduce Scion to the U.S. market after Toyota's sub-brand folded over ten years ago. The company says that the KEI-01 will be assembled at Toyota's Indiana plant in the second half of 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Tesla Model Y left a parkway in El Dorado Hills, California, hit a tree and burst into flames in September, killing three of the four people inside.
  • The crash was widely covered in the Sacramento area as a fiery single-car wreck.
  • Late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Tesla Model Y left a parkway in El Dorado Hills, California, hit a tree and burst into flames in September, killing three of the four people inside. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, with the car doing 74 mph.

The crash was widely covered in the Sacramento area as a fiery single-car wreck. None of that coverage mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

Late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway. That’s a residential part of the Serrano community in El Dorado Hills, east of Sacramento.

Sources indicate that according to the CHP’s Placerville office, the Model Y left the road “for unknown reasons,” hit a tree on the north side of the parkway, and caught fire. Officers got the call around 10:38 p.m. By the time they arrived, the car was fully engulfed in flames.

Industry observers note that charles Anthony Cameron, 30, of Sacramento, was thrown from the car and died at the scene. Alejandra Mendoza, 28, of Sacramento, and Kailauna Viola Mills, 28, of Roseville, were found dead inside once firefighters put out the fire. One of the two women was driving; CHP hasn’t publicly mentioned which.

According to recent reports, mills lived in Arizona and was visiting family. Her uncle told CBS Sacramento she worked in the medical field and was supposed to get married next April.

A fourth person, a 28-year-old Sacramento woman, survived with major injuries.

In a recent development, CHP says the cause is still under investigation. Speed, impairment, and how the car left the road haven’t been released. And nobody has said a word about Autopilot.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

According to recent reports, it lists a 2024 Model Y, a consumer vehicle, and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That’s Tesla confirming through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 74 mph, a fatality, and the California Highway Patrol as the investigating agency.

Then it redacts the narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

The rest of the report is strangely thin. Tesla lists the roadway type as “Unknown” and what the car hit as “Unknown,” even though police said it was a tree. It checks only one source for how it learned of the crash: the media. So Tesla found out about a triple-fatal crash in one of its cars from the news, then went into its own data and confirmed its driver-assist was on.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 05:36 UTC, which is 10:36 p.m. Pacific on September 12, within two minutes of the 10:38 p.m. call CHP responded to. The city, the 2024 Model Y, the month, and the fatal outcome all line up. It’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report from El Dorado Hills in the data. It’s the same crash.

In a recent development, two of the three victims were found inside the car after the fire was out. The survivor got out of, or was pulled from, the wreckage, depending on the report.

CHP hasn’t said whether the doors played any role, and we’re not suggesting they did. But it’s a fair question to ask about any Tesla crash with a fire, now that NHTSA is writing newly introduced rules for emergency door releases after years of complaints about people getting trapped. We’ve asked.

This is the second triple-fatal crash in Tesla’s latest NHTSA filings where its driver-assist was verified engaged and the public never heard about it. The other one was on I-75 in Naples. Add Vineland and July’s four fatal crashes, and the pattern is hard to miss.

But it couldn’t fill in what the car hit, and it learned about three deaths in one of its cars from the news. Then it redacted the one field, the narrative, that would tell us what the car did.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that but these leftovers aren’t all space junk.
  • A significant chunk of the space trash on the moon consists of old landing gear from previous moon visits, Aidan Cowley, a science officer at the European Space Agency, tells Popular Science.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that since the Soviet Union’s Luna 2 probe crashed into the moon’s surface in 1959, the first-ever human-made object to reach the moon, humanity has racked up over 140 missions to our only natural satellite. These missions have delivered 12 humans, seven lunar rovers, and 412,000 pounds (187,000 kilograms) of discarded materials to the moon’s surface. That’s the weight of a Boeing 747 passenger plane.

Sources indicate that but these leftovers aren’t all space junk. In fact, some of this debris may prove useful for future lunar exploration.

A significant chunk of the space trash on the moon consists of old landing gear from previous moon visits, Aidan Cowley, a science officer at the European Space Agency, tells Popular Science.

Recent findings suggest that early moon exploration missions, like NASA’s Apollo missions, would land on the moon using a non-reusable lunar module, says Cowley. “It would land, and then the top part of that module would return back to lunar orbit to rendezvous with the command module and return back to Earth. So, the base part of this vehicle would remain.”.

Leftover lunar rovers—manned or unmanned land vehicles used to explore the moon’s surface—also contribute to the growing mass of junk. These include China’s robotic Yutu rover, which sent information back to Earth for 31 months, as well as those that crash-landed, like the United Arab Emirates’s Rashid rover.

It has been revealed that other trash on the moon includes scientific equipment, toolboxes, and lunar impactor probes. These are devices that smash into the moon’s surface, not by accident, but to fulfill specific objectives, like close-up imaging or to fire rocks and dust into the air for analysis.

Images of the moon’s barren landscape might make you think that these lunar leftovers simply sit around undisturbed until the visit of the next crewed mission. But that’s not the case.

It has been revealed that the moon is an incredibly harsh environment. It’s “constantly bombarded with micrometeorites,” explains Cowley. These tiny rock chunks, along with intense radiation, sunlight exposure, and dramatic temperature swings, will steadily wear down and damage objects.

The iconic American flag planted on the moon by Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin in 1969, for example, has likely been bleached almost white by the sun.

It has been revealed that but some of this damaged, degraded material could still have value for future moon exploration. Cowley states samples of human equipment on the moon could be assessed to understand how the environment alters them.

Studying the impact of micrometeorites on equipment, for example, “might allow us to produce better solar cell or solar panel protection, so they don’t get degraded for humans when humans may eventually live on the moon,” says Cowley.

In 1960, scientists predicted the world would end on November 13, 2026.

Why can’t we just launch all of Earth’s garbage into the sun?

Ahead of plans by NASA and the China National Space Agency to send crewed missions to the moon in the next five years, more equipment will likely amass on the lunar surface. But there are reasons to think these future missions may leave less of a mess behind.

“You might see more emphasis these days on vehicles that have a reusable aspect,” indicates Cowley. “Maybe the lander can land as one unit and take off as one unit again,” he says. Spaceships in development like SpaceX’s Starship Human Landing System (HLS) strategy to adopt this reusable design.

Even if more equipment doesn’t accumulate on the moon, Cowley says the ESA has made prepares to reuse some of this moon trash. One project has explored the potential of 3D printing methods to incorporate lunar scrap into latest materials. Such efforts will have to account for the likelihood that such materials will be contaminated by lunar dust—sharp, shard-like particles of the rocky lunar surface that can prove a further hazard to machinery.

Cowley indicates that the lightweight aluminum that makes up the shell of many lunar vehicles could be melted down using concentrated sunlight.

“Rather than bringing things here with you or mining them on the moon,” says Cowley, “you could actually just reuse the old equipment in the same way we recycle stuff down here on Earth.”.

In a recent development, that lunar “junk” may prove invaluable to the first humans to one day call the moon home. Or, as the old saying goes, one person’s trash is another person’s treasure.

Sources indicate that the T4X will be the first to go on sale (targeting late 2028) according to the brand, and it has a two-seat cab with a steel drop-side flatbed. Mentioned bed measures 79.1 inches long and 70.6 inches wide. The tailgate has some neat features with integrated cup holders, recesses for phones or tablets, and bottle openers on either side.

The T4C crew cab trades some of the bed length for passenger space, as it seats up to five people. That noted, the bed is still fairly long, at 54.1 inches in length.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, the S4C seats six, and notably has a shorter rear overhang than the trucks to help with the departure angle for off-roading. The cargo area can be accessed via a side-hinged tailgate, and the rear glass even drops down into the door.

Sources indicate that these are the unique body style features REO is detailing for now, but they all have much more in common than they do differences. For example, each REO vehicle will be equipped with a naturally aspirated four-cylinder engine that the company notes is designed for longevity, drive-ability and towing more than outright performance. A six-speed manual transmission comes standard, while a six-speed automatic gearbox will be optional. Every REO is also fitted with part-time four-wheel drive, allowing you to select 2WD or 4WD High/Low via a floor-mounted lever. A locking rear differential will be optional for those who want it.

Expect a bumpy ride, because in addition to the body-on-frame construction, all REOs will have solid axles front and rear. Disc brakes will be fitted up front, but drums are used in the back. You’ll steer with hydraulic assistance, and 17-inch steel wheels will be wrapped by all-season tires. Should off-roading be in your future, a “Ransom Package” will be optional, adding off-road tires with unique off-road wheels, upgraded dampers/leaf springs, and a 2.5-inch suspension lift. (You’ll also get orange accents that designate it as the Ransom Package model.).

Photos of the interior aren’t available, but REO indicates physical controls will “take prominence.” Unlike the Slate Truck, power windows come standard, but the seats are manually adjustable. There will still be screens, though, as REO says it comes with a digital cluster and display for navigation and media.

In a recent development, as of now, the T4X is slated to start at $21,500 and be sold in a direct-sales model (no dealers). The T4C is meant to starts at $25,000, and the S4C at $28,500. The manufacturer says it aims to assemble all three in Texas. While the T4X is meant to reach buyers in late 2028, neither the crew cab pickup nor the SUV have predicted on-sale dates yet; if you want one, REO is taking refundable $25 deposits.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

Tennis is Aces for Healthy Aging

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (790 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if we told you tennis has been shown to boost heart health, balance, strength, mental acuity, and mood plus add nearly 10 years to your life, you might think we also had a bridge to sell you.
  • “Tennis is a whole-body sport,” claims sports medicine surgeon Alexis Colvin, MD, chief medical officer of the US Open.
  • Sources indicate that you also don’t have to be a star tennis player to reap the longevity benefits, Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if we told you tennis has been shown to boost heart health, balance, strength, mental acuity, and mood plus add nearly 10 years to your life, you might think we also had a bridge to sell you. But it’s true: Research highlights that even recreational tennis can have a seriously impressive impact on your health—now and for years to come.

“Tennis is a whole-body sport,” claims sports medicine surgeon Alexis Colvin, MD, chief medical officer of the US Open. “It offers cardiovascular benefits, muscle strengthening, flexibility—all the things you need to deal with any physical challenges later in life.”.

Sources indicate that you also don’t have to be a star tennis player to reap the longevity benefits, Dr. Colvin adds. In a 2020 study she co-authored, researchers surveyed over 10,000 tennis players, most of them recreational; about 70 percent played just one to three days a week. The players scored higher than the general population on measures such as physical strength, mental and emotional health, and social engagement. “You don't have to be playing at a very high level to get those benefits,” Dr. Colvin says.

According to recent reports, and those benefits appear to extend one’s life: When researchers followed 8,577 people for up to 25 years, they found that those who played tennis an average of 103 minutes a week lived 9.7 years longer than their sedentary counterparts. They also lived significantly longer than cyclists (who get an extra 3.7 years), swimmers (3.4 years), and joggers (3.2 years).

Even if you’ve never played tennis before, it’s never too late to start. Keep reading for five reasons to pick up a racket, hit the court, and do your future self a favor.

Tennis involves bursts of high intensity movement—sprinting to the net, running backwards to lob a volley, stopping and then lunging to the opposite side of the court to hit the ball—all of which can do wonders for your cardiovascular health. It boosts heart rate, maximizes your body’s use of oxygen, strengthens heart muscle, improves circulation, and can lower blood pressure and cholesterol levels. As a result, women who play tennis an average two to three hours a week have a 44 percent lower risk of developing cardiovascular disease and a 66 percent lower chance of dying from it.

When you sprint across the court, swing a racquet, or come to a sudden stop, you’re working your leg muscles, core, shoulders, back, and arms—in other words, strengthening nearly every part of the body. A recent study of more than 5,000 women between the ages 63 and 99 found that those who had greater muscle strength lived the longest. And because you’re also supporting your own body weight as you run and land, the sport also helps increase bone density, Dr. Colvin indicates. Stronger bones mean a lower risk of fractures and osteoporosis in the future, which is what you need if you want to age well.

According to recent reports, tennis requires coordinated movement and muscle control to maintain fluid footwork and smooth, continuous swings. Your core helps make that possible and is key to good balance. Both core strength and balance can help you avoid falls and fractures as you get older. Another part of balance is visuospatial skill—the ability to recognize environmental cues that help you stay upright. Tennis may help sharpen that, too. In a 2022 study, older tennis players who faced a disruption that could throw them off balance were able to react and steady themselves as well as younger players.

Sources indicate that tennis demands intense focus and decision making. “There’s a lot of active thinking going on,” Dr. Colvin says. “You’re making a lot of split-second decisions while you’re playing, plus thinking about the overall strategy of the game. That kind of mental engagement is crucial as we get older.” According to research, engaging in that kind of quick and strategic thinking while being physically active may be particularly good at promoting neuroplasticity and boosting cognitive function—both of which can stave off the cognitive decline that can come with age.

Studies have found that people who play tennis regularly tend to be less stressed or anxious than people who do lower-intensity exercise. They also report feeling more optimistic, less depressed, and a greater sense of well-being. Like other high-energy sports, tennis may boost mood by prompting the release of brain chemicals such as endorphins, dopamine, and serotonin. It’s also a fun game to play with friends. “The social aspect of tennis is one of its key benefits,” Dr. Colvin says. Numerous studies show that those kinds of community ties are essential for a long, healthy, happier life. With tennis, that’s built into the game.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • This upcoming food pyramid emphasizes plant-based protein sources, cooking with plant-based oils, and healthier sugars and carbohydrates.
  • It also echoes the traditional food pyramid used in the United States since 1992.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A first-of-its-kind international food pyramid, developed by 22 leading nutritionists from Europe, Canada, the United States, and Australia, was published in Advances in Nutrition in September.

This upcoming food pyramid emphasizes plant-based protein sources, cooking with plant-based oils, and healthier sugars and carbohydrates.

It also echoes the traditional food pyramid used in the United States since 1992.

The new pyramid breaks away from the Trump administration’s updated nutritional guidelines, which are part of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Health Again (MAHA) agenda and prioritize red meat over plants.

The new pyramid was designed by a research team led by Brigham Young University professor Karen Della Corte. The researchers noted that this is the first international food pyramid that is designed to reflect scientific agreement across multiple countries and cultures.

Della Corte and researchers from the International Carbohydrate Quality Consortium (ICQC), compared dietary guidelines from multiple countries, including:.

They also analyzed evidence from more than 250 scientific publications, while drawing on the EAT-Lancet Planetary Health Diet to identify principles of healthy eating that may be shared.

The new pyramid highlights three guidelines:.

While the pyramid emphasizes plant-based proteins, it doesn’t exclude animal proteins.

“I find the newly introduced international food pyramid a more practical and aligned approach for the prevention of chronic disease,” mentioned Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the creation of the food pyramid.

“The latest international food pyramid places greater emphasis on food quality and the importance of building meals around nutrient-dense plant foods, while still allowing room for lean animal proteins such as fish, poultry, eggs, and yogurt,” she added.

While the upcoming pyramid and the current U.S. dietary guidelines differ in many ways, they also agree on certain factors.

For example, both sets of guidelines discourage added sugars, refined carbs, and highly processed snacks.

The differences between the two mainly lie in their emphasis on specific sources of protein and fat. For example, the new pyramid prioritizes plant-based proteins, while the U.S. guidelines place greater emphasis on animal proteins, including red meat.

While both sets of recommendations advise limiting saturated fat, the newly introduced pyramid emphasizes unsaturated plant oils, whereas the U.S. guidelines also include butter and beef tallow as cooking fat options.

According to recent reports, routhenstein noted that an key distinction is that this new pyramid goes beyond simply telling people to eat more protein or fewer carbohydrates. Instead, it encourages people to consider the quality and sources of those nutrients.

However, the main emphasis of both guidelines is encouraging people to eat fewer ultra-processed foods and more natural or “real” foods.

Routhenstein told Healthline that research consistently shows that plant-forward eating patterns, including the Mediterranean and DASH diets, are associated with better cardiovascular health and a lower risk of heart disease.

Plant foods provide fiber, potassium, antioxidants, and other beneficial compounds that can help support healthy cholesterol levels, blood pressure, blood sugar, and blood vessel function.

“This is not to say that protein and fat are unimportant, but their sources matter,” Routhenstein remarked.

In a statement from BYU, Della Corte shared the following tips for incorporating the new pyramid’s recommendations into your diet:.

Industry observers note that the pyramid is a framework, not a personalized prescription. If you have questions about your individual nutritional needs, you can speak with your healthcare professional or a licensed dietitian.

“It is key to recognize that plant-forward does not mean vegan or vegetarian. The amount and sources of animal protein should be considered to ensure they align with an individual’s cardiometabolic goals and lab targets,” Routhenstein said.

9 rescued orangutans returned to the wild in Indonesia

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the Indonesian province of West Kalimantan, on the island of Borneo, is no stranger to wildfires.
  • Earlier this year, four mother-baby orangutan pairs and one adult female orangutan (genus Pongo) were rescued from areas in Ketapang (a regency in the West Kalimantan province) impacted by the fires.
  • They were taken to an orangutan rescue and rehabilitation centre in Ketapang, West Kalimantan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Indonesian province of West Kalimantan, on the island of Borneo, is no stranger to wildfires. Horrific wildfires burned in 2015 and 2019, the latter of which set ablaze around 1.6 million hectares of Indonesian forest and land. However, the scale of destruction from this year’s El Niño-intensified fires throughout the island is unprecedented, according to the nonprofit International Animal Rescue.

Earlier this year, four mother-baby orangutan pairs and one adult female orangutan (genus Pongo) were rescued from areas in Ketapang (a regency in the West Kalimantan province) impacted by the fires. They were dehydrated and malnourished, and some had burned their feet, likely because they stepped on embers as they crossed burning peatland.

They were taken to an orangutan rescue and rehabilitation centre in Ketapang, West Kalimantan. The center is run by Yayasan Inisiasi Alam Rehabilitasi Indonesia (YIARI), a nonprofit dedicated to primate and habitat conservation in Indonesia. YIARI’s medical team kept an eye on their recovery, and then conducted health examinations to make sure they were all ready for release. The last of these examinations revealed that three of the females were pregnant.

“Their return to the wild is therefore especially notable, giving these mothers the opportunity to raise their future young in a safer forest habitat,” International Animal Rescue, YIARI’s founding partner, wrote in a statement.

Experts ultimately chose to release them at Batu Nyambu Protected Forest. While also in West Kalimantan, its roughly 23,000 hectares of land and nearby forests haven’t been affected by the recent fires. Batu Nyambu has plenty of natural food, fresh water, nesting trees, and space. But getting the females and their babies there wasn’t simple—they had to travel by road, boat, and on foot for a total of 12 hours. Luckily, they had support from local communities and traditional leaders.

It has been revealed that “We are grateful for the support of the community, village governments and traditional leaders,” said Argitoe Ranting, YIARI’s Director of Operations. “The long-term success of conservation efforts depends not only on protecting the area, but also on the role of the people living around the forest in safeguarding habitat and preventing various threats to wildlife.”.

Most fires in Indonesia are associated with human activity such as using fire to clear land for plantations and agriculture.

According to recent reports, november through New Year’s is marketed as the magical season, and for many people, it can be. But if you are struggling with infertility and/or pregnancy loss, it can represent two months of triggers, traumas, jealousy, and misery. Why? Lots of reasons.

In a recent development, many people save surprise pregnancy announcements for gatherings, which can be agonizing for anyone who wants nothing more than to make such an announcement themselves. Family and friend parties bring forced encounters. Intrusive questions are common: So when are you going to start a family? I hear you’ve been struggling. I think you should see my cousin’s doctor. You need to gain weight, exercise less, try my herbalist, or just adopt.

And it doesn't help when the focus of TV specials, commercials, and religious services is on babies and children. What can you do to make this season a bit less dread-worthy? Maybe even experience some joy?

Don’t assume that every pregnancy announcement or belly was achieved easily or through spontaneous sex (roughly 1 in every 37 babies are conceived through IVF). Many people never share their infertility struggles, and most of those who build their families through donor eggs, sperm, or embryo don’t tell anyone.

You are not alone. It is estimated that 1 in 6 individuals struggle with family-building.

According to recent reports, if you can’t get into the holiday mood whatsoever, don’t pressure yourself. The majority of those experiencing infertility report symptoms of anxiety and depression, and women experience the same level of psychological distress as do women facing cancer or heart disease.

Most importantly, put yourself on your own list; nurture yourself.

In a recent development, resolve is the National Infertility Organization. They provide patient education and support in every state.

Prelude patients also have access to emotional support information/resources on their patient portal.

Recent findings suggest that ASRM is the American Society for Reproductive Medicine. They provide up-to-date, accurate medical information.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you spend your nights dreaming of rally cars but the need for a practical daily driver keeps your automotive wishlist grounded in reality, the Toyota GR Corolla might be your magic bullet. Paired with a motorsport-derived all-wheel-drive system, the GR Corolla's turbocharged 1.6-liter three-cylinder is a firecracker of an engine that churns out 300 horsepower in a frenzy. A six-speed manual transmission comes standard, but a quick-shifting eight-speed automatic transmission with steering-wheel-mounted paddles is also available.

Despite its racy attitude, the GR is still a Corolla hatchback underneath. That means that its interior is comfortable, contemporary, and simply appointed, and its rear hatch lifts to expose a healthy amount of cargo space. With both fun and practicality quotients maxed out, the GR Corolla executes the hot-hatch vision expertly.

Expert Tip: The GR Corolla's primary competitors include the Honda Civic Type R and the Volkswagen Golf R. Those models are more expensive, but both the Civic and Golf beat the GR Corolla in a three-car comparison test that we conducted in 2023.

Sources indicate that for 2026, Toyota has cooked up something special for the track rats. A GRMN Corolla joins the lineup with more aggressive bodywork, race-tuned suspension, and slightly more torque for better performance on the racetrack.

According to recent reports, carbon fiber bodywork—including a unique hood, an adjustable rear wing, and a unique hood—reduce weight while also providing additional downforce. The GRMN also makes use of a race-tuned suspension setup, featuring new front and rear monotube dampers with rebound springs. Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 tires come standard.

Other speed-focused improvements to the GRMN include a bump in torque to 302 pound-feet, a rear-seat delete, tuning adjustments to the electric power steering and the all-wheel-drive system, and a newly introduced intercooler spray system to keep the engine cool after repeated hot laps.

If this year's model is largely unchanged and you're comfortable with a lightly used car, you may want to consider shopping previous model years. A one-to-three-year-old model will likely have a warranty and it'll cost less than buying fresh.

Our new comparison tool provides a comprehensive, side-by-side comparison of up to five vehicles of your choice.

Under the hood of the GR Corolla is a turbocharged three-cylinder engine plucked from Toyota's GR Yaris—a tiny hatchback that the Japanese automaker sells in global markets outside of the United States. For the GR Corolla, it has been tuned to make 300 horsepower. Buyers have the option of either a six-speed manual gearbox or eight-speed automatic with paddle shifters, and all models come with an adjustable all-wheel-drive system.

The GR-Four system allows the driver to choose among different power-distribution modes, starting with a 60/40 front-to-rear power split for everyday driving to up to 30/70 to allow for drifting antics; a 50/50 split option is intended to provide maximum traction for track driving.

Cornering grip is tenacious, and on a twisty road, the GR Corolla rewards its driver with a memorable blend of sure-footedness and civility. While pedal placement makes heel-toe downshifts difficult, the six-speed manual is otherwise easy to row; a rev-match feature is standard to smooth those downshifts. We drove the automatic version and found that it offers quick shifts and a responsive feel, plus a more relaxed demeanor when cruising on the highway. We also drove the GRMN version and were impressed with its track capabilities.

Car and Driver calculates your car's value in three free and easy steps - using the same Black Book® data dealers use to appraise vehicles.

Recent findings suggest that in Comparison: In a sprint to 60 mph, the 2026 GR Corolla manual we tested was quicker than the more powerful Volkswagen Golf R, which managed a 4.6-second run in our testing. Opting for the automatic will tack on an additional 0.8 second to the manual Corolla's 60 mph time.

According to recent reports, the EPA estimates the GR Corolla's fuel economy when fitted with the six-speed manual at 21 mpg city and 28 mpg highway. Equipped with the 8-speed automatic, those numbers fall to 19 mpg city and 27 mpg highway.

Sources indicate that on our 75-mph highway fuel economy route, a manual-transmission GR Corolla delivered 28 mpg; an automatic-equipped model returned an impressive 35 mpg. For more information about the GR Corolla's fuel economy, visit the EPA's website.

First Row: The GR Corolla shares most of its cabin with the standard Corolla hatchback, which means good build quality, a smattering of soft-touch materials, and plenty of features. The interior is upgraded with racier trim and sport seats. Standard equipment includes ambient interior lighting, a six-way adjustable driver's seat, push-button start, and aluminum pedal covers.

Sources indicate that second Row: Like the standard Corolla hatchback, space in the GR Corolla's second row is passable but not roomy. The Volkswagen Golf R provides significantly more head and legroom for rear seat passengers.

Cargo Capacity: In our testing, we were able to fit three carry-on suitcases under the GR Corolla's rear hatch with the rear seats in their upright position. With the second row folded flat, we managed to squeeze 15 carry-on bags into the cargo hold.

Industry observers note that an 8.0-inch infotainment display with Apple CarPlay and Android Auto is standard and also includes Amazon Alexa capability and an onboard Wi-Fi hotspot. The top-tier Premium Plus trim adds a nine-speaker JBL stereo system with an Active Sound Control feature, which pumps fake engine noise into the cabin.

Toyota currently offers much of its driver-assistance technology as standard on most of its lineup, and the GR Corolla is no different. A host of desirable tech features are bundled together across the lineup and include adaptive cruise control, pedestrian and cyclist detection, and automatic high-beam headlamps.

For information about the GR Corolla's crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites.

Recent findings suggest that like other Toyotas, the GR Corolla comes with a standard warranty package enhanced by a two-year complimentary scheduled maintenance plan. All GR Corollas come with a one-year membership to the National Auto Sport Association, a sanctioning body that conducts sports car races across the U.S. The membership includes access to a complimentary high-performance driving class. If you buy a GR Corolla, take the class; you'll love it.

#52322. Pearley: How the Saab 99 Turbo Changed the World

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1199 w)

Pearley: How the Saab 99 Turbo Changed the World

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1199 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Roadandtrack

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it didn’t seem so at the time, but 1977 would prove to be among the most important years in automotive history.
  • In a recent development, yeah, Saab isn’t around today; there were turbocharged cars built before it; and the 99 never sold in overwhelming numbers (at least not here in America).
  • In a recent development, the 99 was already ancient by 1977.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it didn’t seem so at the time, but 1977 would prove to be among the most important years in automotive history. Commercially, this was the model year when General Motors “downsized” its full-size cars from gargantuan to merely huge. Their immense sales success meant the era of land dreadnoughts was over. It was the first model year for the BMW 3-Series name in America and the first for the Porsche 924, that organization’s first front-engine car. In Formula One, Colin Chapman introduced ground effects aerodynamics to the series with the revolutionary Lotus 78. Culturally, 1977 was the year of Smokey and the Bandit, which continues to define what a silly car chase movie must be. But quite sneakily, with 50 years of hindsight, the most important development of 1977 was the introduction of the Saab 99 Turbo.

In a recent development, yeah, Saab isn’t around today; there were turbocharged cars built before it; and the 99 never sold in overwhelming numbers (at least not here in America). But almost every car for sale today derives at least some of its essence from that eccentric Swedish front-driver. “Saab’s use of a turbocharger differs considerably from that of other car makers, such as Porsche,” reported John Lamm in Road & Track’s October 1977 road test. “[I]n that Saab’s goal is maximum torque at mid-range engine speeds rather than dramatic boost at high output.”.

In a recent development, the 99 was already ancient by 1977. Originally shown in 1967 as Saab’s first stretch beyond dinky cars with weird two-stroke engines, it went into production in 1968 as a 1969 model and was, by Saab’s standards, a hit. But it was still weird—wraparound windshield, odd ducky styling, and yeah, the ignition key was down behind the shifter—and at a time when front-wheel drive was rare, it was front-drive.

According to recent reports, saab’s buyers had a certain academic and liberal edge, too. According to researchers at the University of Connecticut and reported by Time magazine in 1976, a staggering 98 percent of Saab owners voted for Democratic candidate George McGovern over Republican incumbent Richard Nixon in the 1972 presidential election. In that election, Nixon carried 60.7 percent of the vote, and won 49 of the 50 states. Saab owners weren’t like everyone else.

It has been revealed that the 99’s “Slant-4” four-cylinder engine was based on the V-8 installed in the British Triumph Stag. By 1972, Saab had taken over production of the engine itself, and had modified the design to be robust and reliable, but there was nothing exotic about what Saab now called the B engine. It had an iron block and a single overhead cam aluminum head. Simple stuff. And in the 1976 99 EMS, the sportiest model in the line, the 2.0-liter eight-valve engine was rated at 115 horsepower channeled through a four-speed manual transmission.

Saab didn’t have the resources to develop a new engine, but it had plenty of turbocharging experience with its Scania large truck division. “The immediate problem,” explained R&T’s Thos. L. Bryant after driving the new 99 Turbo in Sweden for the December 1976 problem, “was to get low-speed torque for the drivability while at the same time limiting high engine speed power for durability.” To achieve that goal, Saab used small turbochargers and advanced electronic engine controls.

Saab already used Bosch K-Jetronic fuel injection on the B engine, and while it wasn’t a wholly electronic system, it was good at advanced fuel metering. And it was the same system Porsche used on the 911 Turbo. Also, Saab developed its own electronic Automatic Performance Control (APC) that used a knock sensor in the block and pressure sensors in the intake manifold to trigger a wastegate and limit turbo boost when the engine couldn’t take any more.

Industry observers note that saab didn’t hide the small, quick-spooling Garrett T3 turbocharger in the 99, putting it forward of the engine. And what was downstream of it was nearly as key. Saab breakthrough emissions tech, known as “Lambda,” ensured that performance could be compatible with stricter emissions controls and catalytic converters. “Basically, Lambda is a 3-component catalyst designed to handle NOx as well as CO and HC,” explained Bryant. “The normal catalytic converter takes care of the last two pollutants fairly well, but NOx usually requires lower compression ratios and exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) to keep it from being passed out through the tailpipe.”.

Lambda added three pieces alongside the fuel injection system: There was an oxygen sensor to monitor air-fuel mixture; an electronic control system that tweaked the air-fuel mixture to keep it close to the ideal stoichiometric value; and a switch on the throttle housing to override the metering system under full-load conditions. It was effective enough so that the engine could meet California’s 1977 emissions without using an Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) valve.

It has been revealed that altogether, those elements and many subtler tweaks meant the 99 Turbo had 135 horsepower aboard. Not a lot by 2026 standards, but a sweet chunk back then. “In all of our discussions about the Saab Turbo,” R&T reported in the October 1977 test, “the one comment that continually surfaced was. ‘It’s so much fun to drive!’ Obviously, with a net horsepower rating up 20 hp to 135 at 5000 rpm (net torque is 160 at 3500 rpm versus 123 lb-ft for the non-turbocharged Saab and that is the more revealing improvement), the Saab Turbo is not going to give the breathtaking acceleration of a Porsche Turbo Carrera, but the performance increase is substantial and worthwhile.” R&T measured the 99 Turbo waltzing to 60 mph in 9.5 seconds, and running the quarter-mile in 17.5 seconds at 80.5 mph. In the context of the time, a solid performance.

The 99 Turbo wasn’t perfect, but showcased how effective turbocharging and electronic engine controls could be. At the same moment GM was using dumb carburetors on its upcoming 1977 turbocharged Buick V-6, Saab was showing how it could be done. Buick would eventually adopt fuel injection and better electronic engine controls to allow its blown V-6 to mature into a legend with the Grand National and GNX. But Saab was there first.Saab died a sad death after some corporate conniptions. But look around at the turbocharged engines that dominate today. All those engines, powering everything from the Honda Civic Type R to the Kia Telluride, are descendants of the Saab 99 Turbo, which went on sale 50 years ago. As one anonymous staff member noted in that first road test, “This to me is one of the waves of the future: small engine with turbocharger for fuel economy and performance coupled with low exhaust emissions. Neat!”.

John Pearley Huffman has been writing about cars since 1990 and is getting okay at it. Besides Road & Track, his work has appeared in Car and Driver, the Latest York Times, and more than 100 automotive publications and websites. A graduate of UC Santa Barbara, he still lives near that campus with his wife and two children. He owns a pair of Toyota Tundras and two dogs. He used to have a Nova and a Camaro.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that they may be small, but bear cubs have a pretty steep learning curve. In Alaska, brown bear (Ursus americanus) cubs have a roughly 50 percent survival rate within their first year, while the black bear (Ursus americanus) cub survival rate can range from 51 to 88 percent, depending on where they live. Cubs must learn how to fish, forage, find shelter, and climb trees to escape predators. Fortunately, biology helps out a bit with climbing. Bears have claws that curve and help them go up the tree and then back down safely.

Industry observers note that one baby black bear who spent time at Anan Creek in southeastern Alaska’s Tongass National Forest demonstrated off those climbing chops in style. The park’s rangers have officially awarded this bear with the 2026 Cutest Climber Award.

In a recent development, “This little cub slipped on his way down but caught himself and hustled right after mom,” the rangers write. “An adorable reminder that even when you lose your footing, you can recover and keep going. A tiny, furry lesson in resilience provided by the bears of Anan.”.

Tongass National Forest’s rangers  are right now awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Sources indicate that tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for tourists on Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

Sources indicate that according to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears. Similar to  their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

According to recent reports, the U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

#52318. Feeling the Pain of Others

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (804 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Feeling the Pain of Others

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (804 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Are you sure your work hasn’t gotten to you?” he asked.
  • I assumed everyone thought this; I asked my question out loud.
  • I had always considered myself self-aware, but this was the first time I saw my work had transformed my engagement with the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma.

“Are you sure your work hasn’t gotten to you?” he asked. We were visiting our family in the Caribbean. We had hiked to the top of the cliffs on a small island, and for a moment the entire family stood quietly together, marveling at the sea. It was an exquisite sight—turquoise water as far as you could see, and a vast, cloudless sky. As we reached the edge of the cliffs, my first thought was, This is unbelievably beautiful. My second thought was, I wonder how many people have killed themselves by jumping off these cliffs.

I assumed everyone thought this; I asked my question out loud. My stepfather-in-law turned to me slowly and asked his question with such sincerity that I finally understood: My work had gotten to me. I didn’t even tell him the rest of my thoughts: Where would the helicopter land? Could it land on the beach, or would it land on this cliff and then they’d belay down? Is there even a Level 1 trauma center in the Caribbean? Would they have to go to Miami? Would they stop you in customs? It was quite a list.

I had always considered myself self-aware, but this was the first time I saw my work had transformed my engagement with the world.

According to recent reports, my jobs had brought me into intimate contact with people who were living close to or experiencing different types of acute trauma. I worked in confidential locations and at large institutions. I worked days, evenings, and graveyard shifts. I worked in local communities, throughout the country, and the world.

Over time, friends, family, and even clients stated I needed a vacation. Otherwise, stop taking everything so seriously. But I could not hear them; I was doing God’s work. They could either step up and help me or step off. I did not need to reflect on myself. I was arrogant, self-righteous, and impassioned, perhaps to the point of selective blindness. I was convinced that I was just fine.

After so many stories of abuse, death, and tragedies, including missing children, deported loved ones, climate disasters, and other nightmares, I had absorbed and accumulated other people’s pain to the point that it had become part of me, and my view of the world had changed. But I finally understood that this exposure to other people’s overwhelm had fundamentally changed me. I did the work for a long time with little ability to integrate my experiences emotionally, cognitively, physically, or spiritually. I suffered from compassion fatigue.

Rather than staying in touch with the heart that was breaking, I started building walls. In my case, this meant I became increasingly cocky. I had no access to humility, which we all need when honestly engaging our own internal process. Rather than acknowledge my own pain and helplessness in the face of things I could not control, I raged at the possible external causes. I sharpened my critique of systems and society. I became more dogmatic, opinionated, and intolerant of other people’s views. It never occurred to me that my anger might in part be functioning as a shield or that I was warding off anguish. A widely held belief: If you’re tough enough, cool enough, and committed enough, you’ll keep on keeping on. You’ll suck it up.

Sources indicate that instead, I began the long haul of making change. I acknowledged the effects of other people’s pain; I made room for my own internal process. Over the years, I gradually let go. This fatigue takes a personal and professional toll.

We are slow to recognize such fatigue as a broad social concern rather than an isolated individual problem—through a job, daily life, or caregiving. It also goes beyond exposure to human suffering; other species and the planet are also in pain.

Industry observers note that I needed a new framework that allowed me to bear witness to suffering without surrendering my ability to live fully—I call the concept trauma stewardship. This refers to the entire conversation: How we are affected over time, how we make sense of, learn from, and ultimately transform, individually and collectively.

In stewardship, we are entrusted with people’s stories and lives, animals’ well-being, and our planet’s health. We understand that this is an honor as well as a responsibility. As stewards, we make room for and honor others’ hardship and suffering, yet we do not assume their pain as our own.

Recent findings suggest that the essayist E. B. White once wrote that the early American author, naturalist, and philosopher Henry Thoreau had perhaps been “torn by two powerful and opposing drives—the desire to enjoy the world, and the urge to set the world straight.”.
